strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (LLaVA-1.5 7B/13B, Qwen2-VL 7B) and hallucination-focused benchmarks (POPE, CHAIR, MMHal-Bench) with general vision-language tasks (MME, SEED-Bench)
Consistent and substantial improvements on hallucination metrics (20.7% on CHAIR, 15.9% on MMHal-Bench) while maintaining general performance
Well-motivated identification of three specific limitations in prior work: visual attention sink, low visual contribution, and cross-modal fusion imbalance
Strong ablation studies (Table 4) validating that both visual enhancement and cross-modal balance components are essential
Low computational overhead (1.13× vs. greedy decoding) with clear latency benchmarking
Quantitative saliency map validation (Table 1) showing 2.2× improvement of shift method over static baseline
Good reproducibility support with detailed implementation details, hyperparameter tuning methodology, and honest limitations discussion
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines established techniques (attention steering via bias injection from Zhang et al. 2023, saliency-based attention guidance from recent work) without significant methodological innovation

Critical unresolved query dependency: method relies on POS tagging for information-rich words, failing on vague/visually-irrelevant/multilingual queries; paper acknowledges but provides no solutions or empirical failure rate analysis

Insufficient layer selection justification: saliency map layer chosen based on only 50 TextVQA examples then applied across different datasets (POPE, CHAIR) without validation; cross-dataset generalization not established
Cross-modal balance coefficient β=1.0 not empirically validated: paper acknowledges 'investigating whether this balance is truly optimal is left for future work,' yet this is a core design choice

Limited direct evaluation of attention sink mitigation: Table 1 evaluates saliency on COCO single-instance objects (non-representative of hallucination), without direct measurement of reduced attention to irrelevant regions during generation
No statistical significance testing despite potential variance in GPT-4.1 scoring (which requires averaging 5 runs); no confidence intervals or p-values provided
Incomplete ablation studies: no justification for top 50% attention head selection, min-max normalization choice, or three standard deviation clipping threshold
Modest improvements on some benchmarks: POPE F1 improvement is only 3.0% (86.0→86.8), limiting practical significance; 13% computational overhead may be problematic for real-time applications
Insufficient generalization analysis: only tested on 7B/13B models with model-specific hyperparameters (α=5.0 vs 4.0); no evaluation on newer models or other architectures
Limited failure mode analysis: Figure 12 shows residual hallucinations but provides no systematic error analysis or breakdown by hallucination type; no comparison of when/why GIFT fails vs baselines

strengths: Clear problem motivation with well-articulated limitations of prior work (attention sink, low visual contribution, imbalanced cross-modal fusion)
Novel gaze shift-based saliency map computation that empirically demonstrates 2.2× improvement over static attention (Table 1) and naturally mitigates attention sink
Addresses important cross-modal fusion balance by proportionally scaling query attention based on visual enhancement (Eq. 7), distinguishing from VAF/VAR
Comprehensive experiments across 4 model architectures, 7 benchmarks, with thorough ablations demonstrating component contributions (up to 25.4% improvement from joint components vs. visual-only)
Strong empirical results: 20.7% improvement on CHAIR, 15.9% on MMHal-Bench, consistent gains across diverse models
Practical efficiency with only 1.13× latency overhead compared to 1.56-11.10× for baselines
Layer selection robustness demonstrated: multiple moderate layer configurations achieve strong performance (Table 6)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, well-organized appendices, and honest limitations discussion
Works across multiple VLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen) without retraining, enabling practical deployment
weaknesses: Limited novelty: attention steering is established; main contribution is saliency map preprocessing; cross-modal balance adjustment is straightforward extension

Significant unresolved limitation: method depends on query tokens to identify visual regions; fails when answers don't require visual information or queries are irrelevant to images; acknowledged but not addressed with default implementation

Inconsistent improvements across metrics: POPE shows only 3.0% improvement vs. 20.7% on CHAIR, suggesting method works better for some hallucination types than others with no analysis of which categories benefit

Overclaimed 'intrinsic' layer selection: tested on only 50 examples, 2 datasets (both visual understanding); different models show different peak layers (11, 10, 14, 18) contradicting universality claim

Insufficient justification for key design choices: exponential scaling in Eq. 6 (why not linear?), clipping at 3σ (no ablation), β fixed to 1.0 ('investigating optimality left for future work' contradicts principled design claims)
Weak statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars; GPT-4.1 scoring variance unreported; Figure 6 shows performance oscillations
Suboptimal default word extraction: POS tagging selected over LLM-based approach despite Table 7 showing better results (52.6 vs 57.3), justified only by 'negligible overhead'
Limited failure analysis: Figure 12 shows remaining hallucinations but no systematic error categorization; missing analysis of when method helps most/least

Metric reliability concerns inadequately addressed: authors acknowledge CHAIR may misrepresent Qwen3-VL 8B's hallucinations as string-matching artifact, yet headline results still emphasize CHAIR gains
Baseline comparison limited: VAF, Rel-Attn, VCD, VAR only on LLaVA-1.5; no Qwen2/3 comparisons for these methods; insufficient implementation details for reproducibility
